analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans working abroad exclude unlimited foreign earnings from U.S. income tax.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have let Americans working abroad exclude all their foreign earnings from U.S. tax, never got a hearing or a vote and died in the Ways and Means Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current tax law, an American who lives and works abroad can exclude a limited amount of foreign earnings from U.S. income tax. This bill would have removed that dollar limit entirely, so no matter how much an American earned working overseas, none of it would be taxed by the United States. The benefit would have grown with income — the biggest winners would be highly paid executives and consultants abroad — while the lost revenue would have to be made up by other taxpayers. The bill never received a hearing, a vote, or any action beyond its referral to the tax-writing committee.
analysis.who_benefits: The direct beneficiaries are American citizens and residents who earn wages or fees abroad. Today they can shield only a capped amount of foreign earnings from U.S. tax (roughly $91,000 in 2009); this bill removes the cap, so the savings are tiny for a modest earner and very large for a highly paid executive or consultant living overseas. Multinational employers also benefit indirectly, since they no longer need to compensate staff for the extra U.S. tax on foreign assignments.

how_it_helps.text: It lets a qualified individual elect to exclude all income earned for work performed in a foreign country, with no dollar cap and no phase-out.
It applies to tax years beginning after enactment, and the largest dollar benefit goes to the highest-paid Americans abroad, since every dollar of foreign salary above the old cap becomes tax-free.

analysis.who_pays: The U.S. Treasury loses the tax revenue on foreign earnings above the current cap, and that shortfall would be borne by other taxpayers — overwhelmingly Americans who live and work in the United States, whose tax bills would be higher than they otherwise would be.

drawbacks.text: An unlimited exclusion benefits high earners the most: an American making $20,000 abroad gains little, while an executive making $500,000 abroad avoids roughly $150,000 or more in federal tax a year, so the tax burden shifts toward ordinary taxpayers who cannot leave the country.
The bill contained no way to make up the lost revenue, and the Joint Tax Committee never scored it because the bill never advanced, so the size of the revenue giveaway was never put on the record.

Supporters of the current cap argue some limit is fair because U.S. citizenship-based taxation already lets exempt workers use foreign credits and services abroad; removing the cap entirely, rather than raising it, gives a windfall to the highest-paid expatriates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill had a real, narrow benefit: Americans working abroad, like Americans competing at home, would have paid tax only where they earned their money, and the change would have removed a barrier to taking overseas assignments. But the cost fell on everyone else. Because there was no dollar cap, the exclusion would have been worth the most to the highest earners, and the revenue they no longer paid would have had to come from other taxpayers or borrowing. The plain drafting — an unlimited exclusion with no income ceiling and no offsetting revenue — made it a tax shift toward the well-off abroad, and the bill drew almost no support and never moved.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Ways and Means Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, and the committee never held a hearing, marked it up, or sent it to the floor.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 30, 2009 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee that writes tax law.
No further action was ever taken: the committee never reported the bill, and it never received a vote in the House before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
The bill attracted only one cosponsor in two years, a single House Republican.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers at home, who would otherwise have picked up the bill for unlimited tax-free foreign earnings by the highest-paid Americans abroad; no revenue was lost.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ordinary taxpayers who would have covered the cost

for.name: Rep. Gregory W. Meeks
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to remove the dollar cap on the foreign earned income exclusion.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further action; the bill died there without a hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes to measure: a House Democrat sponsored it, a single House Republican cosponsored it, and neither chamber ever acted on it.

industries.industry: High-earning U.S. citizens working abroad (executives, consultants, contractors)
industries.note: They would owe no U.S. income tax on any amount of foreign salary, a benefit that scales directly with income. Their gain is the public's cost, because the revenue would be shifted to taxpayers at home.
Sending staff overseas becomes cheaper because firms no longer need to gross up employees' pay for the extra U.S. tax on foreign assignments, lowering the cost of running global operations.
The unlimited exclusion would remove tax on the highest foreign salaries, shrinking federal revenue and leaving the shortfall to be made up by other taxpayers or borrowing.
